newsitem.title: BELGIUM: ALLIANCES NOT TAKEOVERS WAY FORWARD FOR RETAILERS.
newsitem.headline: ALLIANCES NOT TAKEOVERS WAY FORWARD FOR RETAILERS.

text.p: Alliances rather than straight takeovers will play a rising part in the future of the retail sector as it copes with increasing globalisation, the head of leading Belgian retailer Delhaize said on Wednesday.
"Food distribution is not capital rich, and alliances can give the same benefits as takeovers but without having to pay the premiums," he told a seminar of Belgian financial analysts.

Vaucleroy said the retail sector would continue to concentrate in the face of globalisation, would need to switch its focus to the developing countries of Asia and Latin America as other economies slowed, and achieve economies of scale.

"It is indisputably the case that it is becoming increasingly difficult to find good commercial sites. Therefore there will be a push towards more concentration to the detriment of smaller businesses," Vaucleroy said.
He noted that in the United States in particular, but parts of Europe as well, the annual increase in retail sales space outstripped both the rise in the population and in the standard of living.
At the same time, increasingly, supply of goods was falling into the hands of a few giant companies, which meant that supermarket chains were facing tougher price negotiations.
"On the shelves you may well see many brands...but frequently they are all owned by one company," he noted.
While planning globally, retailers could only overlook local needs at their own peril, Vaucleroy said.
"Think global but act local," he said. "We must increasingly have a global strategy but never forget that food products are a local business.
Retailers, particularly in the food sector, had also to pay close attention to the demands and lifestyles of their consumers.
Vaucleroy said that in the United States in particular supermarkets had ignored the growth in convenience foods and consequently paid the price.

"We call this 'the market of the stomach'," Vaucleroy said, noting that in the United States and some parts of Europe the average time spent on food preparation in the home was just 15 minutes per day.
